title: Faithful, Yet Defeated
overview: The people remember God's past help, then protest that they have been crushed and shamed even though they stayed loyal, and beg God to wake up and save them.

parts.label: Stories of past victories (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The people recall what their ancestors told them about God bringing Israel into the land of Canaan by driving out and crushing the nations who lived there. The poem frankly credits that conquest to God's power and favor, not to Israel's own army.

parts.label: Trust in God, not weapons (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: The singer calls God 'my King' and says victory comes from God, not from bow or sword, picturing enemies pushed down the way an ox shoves with its horns. The section ends in confident, lasting praise.

parts.label: But now, defeat and shame (vv. 9-16)
parts.note: The tone flips: the army has lost, people are plundered, scattered and mocked, and God seems to have 'sold' them as if they were worth nothing. Scholars are unsure which of Israel's several defeats this describes.

parts.label: We did not deserve this (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: Unusually, the people insist this did not happen because they left God or prayed to other gods, and they say they suffer 'for your sake' among ruins fit only for jackals. Christians later read verse 22 as describing believers persecuted for their faith, as Paul quotes it in Romans 8.

parts.label: Wake up and help (vv. 23-26)
parts.note: The psalm boldly asks why God is asleep and hiding, a blunt way of speaking to God found in other psalms too. It ends unresolved, face down in the dust, appealing only to God's steady, loyal love.

think: When something bad happens to someone who did nothing to deserve it, what explanations, if any, feel honest to you?
